claims.text: Exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres induces preferential surface segregation of Cr in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Si or Al preferentially segregates to the surface alongside Cr under these exposure conditions.
Segregation of Cr together with Si or Al facilitates formation of a dense, coherent oxide scale with low lattice mismatch.
Mn-containing alloys tend to form unstable oxide layers that crack or spall.
CrFeCoNi alloys lacking Si or Al tend to form unstable oxide layers that crack or spall.
Selective oxidation drives Cr, Si, or Al toward the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched Cr, Si, or Al forms an integrated Cr-rich inner oxide augmented by secondary oxide phases.
The proposed composite oxide structure reduces interfacial stress and mismatch strain.
Reduced interfacial stress and mismatch strain enhance oxide-scale adhesion.
Mn does not produce the beneficial oxide characteristics attributed to Si or Al.
Si- or Al-containing alloys will form thinner oxide layers than Mn-containing alloys and CrFeCoNi controls under the same conditions.
Si- or Al-containing alloys will form more uniform and adherent oxide layers than Mn-containing alloys and CrFeCoNi controls.
Si- or Al-containing alloys will exhibit less oxide cracking and spallation than Mn-containing alloys and CrFeCoNi controls.
The proposed behavior applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed above 900 °C.
The behavior may differ below 900 °C or in alloys with non-equilibrium microstructures.
CrFeCoNi and Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys are proposed as controls exposed under the same conditions as the Si- and Al-containing alloys.
Failure of Si- or Al-containing alloys to show significantly thinner, more uniform, more adherent, and less damaged scales than both controls would falsify the hypothesis.
